description: Looking to work with people who are creative, committed and bring different perspectives to the team! Hope to build a team where everyone brings something meaningful to the table!
summary: ORBIT is an interactive web app that turns 21 years (2005–2025) of NASA Earth observations into clear answers about Punjab, Pakistan. It tracks three variables: Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD), Ultraviolet Aerosol Index (UVAI), and surface albedo. We found (among other things) that winter haze is rising significantly and that the land surface is getting darker, trapping more heat. ORBIT shows this through interactive maps, charts, a glossary and a built-in AI guide, so anyone can explore the science, not just scientists.
details:
ORBIT lets users see how the variables mentioned above have changed in Punjab over time. 

Features and content include:

  • Slider maps: drag through 2005–2025, or press play, to watch haze, smoke and dust, and surface brightness change across the region. “Then vs now” and trend views also show where things are changing.
  • Plain-language summaries of each variable’s direction.
  • What the findings mean for people’s health, food, energy and heat
  • Analysis page: trends, rates of change and significance tests, written in plain language first, with a toggle to show the full science 
  • Interactive scatter plots with guided explanation points.
  • Glossary and ORBIT chatbot: 101 concepts explained, and an AI assistant that answers in plain, mixed or scientific language
  • Open science: downloadable data, PDF summaries and a record of how every chart was made

How it works:

  1. Data collection/cleaning: we downloaded NASA satellite and modelled data for the Punjab region through NASA Giovanni and cleaned it by removing missing values and known sensor errors using the Hampel filter
  2. Detection: we removed the natural seasonal cycle, then tested for real long-term trends using standard climate statistics (seasonal Mann-Kendall, Sen’s slope and trend lines with confidence bands).
  3. Explanation: the results go into the app as interactive maps, charts and plain-English explanations.

Findings:

  • Haze (AOD) is rising, fastest in winter (in the same season as Punjab’s smog emergencies)
  • Smoke and dust (UV Aerosol Index) are rising in winter, a second, independent instrument confirming the winter signal.
  • Surface albedo is decreasing: the ground is getting darker and absorbing more heat.
  • Monsoon haze, mostly natural dust, hasn’t changed. The rise is concentrated in the season of human-made pollution.

Impact/utility:

  • Health: shows the long-term trend behind a smog crisis that cuts from life expectancy 
  • Coverage: satellites see every district back to 2005, including places with no air-quality monitors
  • Food and energy: haze cuts the sunlight reaching crops and solar panels, which matters for Pakistan’s breadbasket and its fast-growing solar power
  • Policy: points action toward winter and its emission sources
  • Accessibility: complex climate data made understandable to students, the public and decision-makers

Limitations and assumptions:

  • Data is regional (roughly 50–100 km grid cells), not street-level
  • Satellites measure haze through the whole air column, not the exact air people breathe.
  • Trends do not show proof of the cause
  • A known OMI sensor fault was filtered out
dataRefs: Surface albedo: MERRA-2 radiation diagnostics (monthly, M2TMNXRAD)
UV Aerosol Index: OMI/Aura OMAERUVd v003
Aerosol Optical Depth: MODIS/Aqua MYD08_M3, Collection 6.1
